routes.name: Northern Silk Road
routes.path: Chang'an → Gansu/Shaanxi → (splits around Taklamakan) → mountain routes north and south → Kashgar → (splits) → Termez/Balkh OR Kokand via Torugart Pass → Karakum Desert → Merv
routes.description: Primary overland route bypassing Taklamakan Desert to the north

routes.name: Southern Silk Road (Karakoram Route)
routes.path: China → Karakoram mountains/Khunjerab Pass → Pakistan → Hindu Kush → Afghanistan → Merv → Iran → Mesopotamia → Levant (Mediterranean) OR branch: Herat → Susa → Charax Spasinu (Persian Gulf) → Petra → Alexandria
routes.description: Mountain route through Hindu Kush and Karakoram, with maritime spurs available

routes.name: Southwestern Route (Ganges-Brahmaputra Route)
routes.path: Sichuan → Yunnan → Burma → Bangladesh → Ganges-Brahmaputra Delta (trading center)
routes.description: Route for bullion (gold and silver) from Yunnan via Burma to maritime termini

routes.name: Central Asian Routes (Iran)
routes.path: Merv → (via Nisa and Sarakhs) → Masshad → Nishapur → Tehran/Ray
routes.description: Persian routes connecting Merv to western Iran

routes.name: Jade Road
routes.description: Earliest route, used since 5000 BCE for jade trade before silk dominance

routes.name: Maritime Silk Road - Eastern Section
routes.path: Southeast Asia → Giao Chỉ (Tonkin Gulf) and Guangzhou (southern China), with secondary routes via Java Sea, Banda Sea, Sulu Sea, Philippines, Taiwan
routes.description: Maritime routes controlled by Austronesian thalassocracies, 2nd century BCE to 15th century CE

routes.name: Maritime Silk Road - Western Section
routes.path: Sumatra/Sunda Strait → Sri Lanka → southern India → Maldives → Arabian Sea → Persian Gulf (Gulf of Oman) or Red Sea (Gulf of Aden) → Mediterranean
routes.description: Primary maritime route crossing Indian Ocean, branches to Persian Gulf and Red Sea

routes.name: Maritime Silk Road - African Branch
routes.path: Arabian Sea coast → East Africa → Zanzibar, Comoros, Madagascar, Seychelles
routes.description: Secondary maritime route along East African coast

routes.name: Steppe Route (Overland, northern steppes)
routes.description: Ancient horse-breeding and nomadic trade routes predating formal Silk Road

routes.name: Han Dynasty Route Consolidation
routes.path: Central Asia → Mediterranean via Tarim Basin and Hexi Corridor connection
routes.description: Route opened by Han Dynasty around 130 BCE with Zhang Qian missions

goods.name: Silk
goods.note: primary commodity; Chinese production; highly lucrative; women's textiles

goods.name: Silk brocade
goods.note: bolts of silk brocade sent in exchange

goods.name: Horses

goods.name: Gold
goods.note: among Western exports; also from Central Asia

goods.name: Jade (nephrite)

goods.name: Spices

goods.name: Roman glassware

goods.name: Gemstones
goods.note: from Thailand and Java via delta

goods.name: Lapis lazuli
goods.note: blue stone from Badakhshan used as paint

goods.name: Sassanid coins
goods.note: Persian currency, valuable as silk yarn and textiles

goods.name: Textiles (Roman)

goods.name: Slaves
goods.note: slave trade connected to Bukhara and Black Sea trades, particularly slave girls

goods.name: Raisins

goods.name: Coffee beans
goods.note: Armenian export from Turkey and Iran (1700-1765)

goods.name: Figs

goods.name: Celadon vases

goods.name: Bullion (gold and silver)

ideas.name: Buddhism
ideas.spread: east→west; 1st century CE onwards; Mahayana, Theravada, Vajrayana forms; major missionary movement
ideas.detail: First large-scale missionary movement; spread to China, Central Asia, Southeast Asia via Kushan empire and merchant support; Buddhist monasteries offered haven and lodging

ideas.name: Christianity (Nestorian)
ideas.spread: west→east; 781 CE stele evidence; spread both east and west simultaneously
ideas.detail: Nestorian Christian monks on Silk Road; missionaries and translators to China

ideas.name: Islam
ideas.spread: west→east; 8th century CE onwards; became dominant by 10th century
ideas.detail: Islamic expansion under Umayyad and Abbasid Caliphates; replaced other religions in Central Asia

ideas.name: Judaism
ideas.spread: west→east; from Mesopotamia eastward post-559 BCE Persian conquest
ideas.detail: Judean merchants (Radanites from Gaul) traded from China to Rome; Khazar Turks facilitated trade

ideas.name: Zoroastrianism
ideas.detail: Ancient Persian religion; spread via Silk Road trade networks; influenced Judaism

ideas.name: Manichaeism
ideas.detail: Spread into Central Asia and China via Silk Road

ideas.name: Syncretism (cultural adaptation)
ideas.spread: both directions; ongoing throughout Silk Road history
ideas.detail: Chinese and Xiongnu adapted military techniques, dress, music, dance from each other; Buddhist monasteries served as cultural centers

ideas.name: Scythian-style animal art
ideas.detail: Chinese jade carvers imitated Scythian designs depicting animals in combat; reflected in belt plaques of gold and bronze

ideas.name: Greco-Buddhist art
ideas.detail: Mixed Greek and Indian elements; Buddha first depicted as human in Kushan period; spread to China via Silk Road

ideas.name: Plague (Black Death)
ideas.detail: Originated in marmots of Central Asia; carried westwards by Silk Road traders; reached Europe via Trebizond; devastated Europe starting late 1340s

ideas.name: Philosophical and scientific thought
ideas.detail: Religious, philosophical, and scientific ideas exchanged alongside goods; often syncretised by societies along routes

chronology.label: Jade trading begins
chronology.detail: Nephrite jade traded from Yarkand and Khotan mines to China

chronology.label: Tarim mummies
chronology.detail: Mummified remains found in Tarim Basin suggest very ancient East-West contacts; possibly Indo-European speakers

chronology.label: Chinese silk in Egypt
chronology.detail: Remnants of Chinese silk found in Ancient Egypt; earliest evidence of silk trade

chronology.label: Gold introduction and Scythian art influence
chronology.detail: Gold introduced from Central Asia; Chinese jade carvers adopt Scythian-style animal art

chronology.label: Elite burial with Greek and Chinese goods
chronology.detail: Burial near Stuttgart contained Greek bronzes and Chinese silks

chronology.label: Persian conquest of Babylon
chronology.detail: Cyrus the Great; Judean slaves freed and dispersed throughout Persian Empire

chronology.label: Emperor Ashoka (Maurya dynasty)
chronology.detail: Converted to Buddhism and raised it to official status in northern India; influenced religion's spread

chronology.label: Han dynasty period
chronology.detail: Initiated and spread Silk Road through exploration and conquests; central to trade development

chronology.label: Silk Road initiation and Zhang Qian missions
chronology.detail: Han dynasty extended control into Central Asia; Zhang Qian visited Dayuan, Yuezhi, Daxia, Kangju; opened Tarim Basin route

chronology.label: Han dynasty expansion into Central Asia
chronology.detail: Emperor Wu ended nomadic tribe harassment; began unified control

chronology.label: Mahayana Buddhism forms
chronology.detail: Mahayana Buddhism developed in northwestern India or Central Asia; became major form spreading east

chronology.label: Roman conquest of Egypt
chronology.detail: Began regular communications and trade between China, Southeast Asia, India, Middle East, Africa, Europe

chronology.label: Battle of Sogdiana
chronology.detail: Han troops encountered and defeated Roman legionaries; Chinese crossbows superior to Roman armor

chronology.label: Silk reaches Rome, Egypt, Greece
chronology.detail: Chinese silk widely sought after in Western Mediterranean; maritime route established

chronology.label: Periplus of the Erythraean Sea written
chronology.detail: Greek 'travel guide' to Indian Ocean trade route by unknown author

chronology.label: Buddhism transmission to China begins
chronology.detail: Semi-legendary account of ambassador sent by Emperor Ming; Mahayana Buddhism enters Han dynasty

chronology.label: Han general Ban Chao secures trade routes
chronology.detail: Led 70,000 mounted troops; expanded conquests to Caspian Sea and Parthia borders; dispatched Gan Ying to Rome (Daqin)

chronology.label: Roman embassies arrive in China
chronology.detail: First recorded embassies during reigns of Marcus Aurelius and Emperor Huan of Han

chronology.label: Extensive Buddhist contact and missionary activity
chronology.detail: Kushan empire expansion into Tarim Basin; Buddhist monks traveled to China; first Parthian, Kushan, Sogdian translators

chronology.label: Buddhist expansion phases
chronology.detail: Dharmaguptakas and Sarvastivadins displaced by Mahayana; Buddhism becomes pan-Asian

chronology.label: Fa-hsien pilgrimage to India
chronology.detail: Chinese pilgrim travels to India for improved Buddhist scripture access

chronology.label: Byzantine Emperor Justinian
chronology.detail: Sent monks as spies to steal silkworm eggs; resulted in Mediterranean silk production; Byzantine monopoly in medieval Europe

chronology.label: Justin II encounters Sogdian embassy
chronology.detail: Byzantine ruler greeted by Sogdian embassy representing Istämi (First Turkic Khaganate); bypassed Sasanian merchants for direct trade

chronology.label: Sui dynasty
chronology.detail: Transitional period between Han decline and Tang resurgence

chronology.label: Tang dynasty golden age
chronology.detail: Tang established second Pax Sinica; Silk Road reached peak; Persian and Sogdian merchants flourished; Chinese maritime presence expanded

chronology.label: Xuanzang pilgrimage
chronology.detail: Chinese pilgrim traveled to India for Buddhist scriptures; fictionalized in Journey to the West (16th century)

chronology.label: Hou Junji conquers Western Regions
chronology.detail: Tang reopened Silk Road; remained open nearly four decades

chronology.label: Byzantine embassy to Tang
chronology.detail: Alleged embassy by Constans II to Emperor Taizong of Tang; recorded in Tang histories

chronology.label: Tibetans capture Silk Road
chronology.detail: Route closed after Tibetan conquest

chronology.label: Silk Road reopened by Tang
chronology.detail: Tang reconquered Four Garrisons of Anxi; reconnected China to West

chronology.label: Tang captures Gilgit Valley
chronology.detail: Vital route control through Gilgit Valley achieved

chronology.label: Tibetans recapture Gilgit Valley
chronology.detail: Loss to Tibetan Empire

chronology.label: Battle of Talas
chronology.detail: Abbasid Caliphate halted Chinese westward expansion near Talas River (modern Kyrgyzstan)

chronology.label: An Lushan Rebellion
chronology.detail: Disastrous rebellion; Tang unable to reassert Central Asia control afterwards

chronology.label: Nestorian Stele created
chronology.detail: Inscribed stele describes introduction of Nestorian Christianity to China

chronology.label: Rise of Islam in Central Asia
chronology.detail: Buddhism transmission essentially ended by 7th century; Islam became dominant

chronology.label: Islamic expansion and Sogdian dominance
chronology.detail: Islamic world expanded under Umayyad Caliphate; Sogdians dominated east-west trade (4th-8th centuries); served as lingua franca

chronology.label: Persian Samanid Empire
chronology.detail: Centered in Bukhara; continued Sogdian trade legacy

chronology.label: Tang reclaims Hexi Corridor
chronology.detail: Tang general Zhang Yichao reclaimed Hexi Corridor and Dunhuang from Tibetans

chronology.label: Song dynasty
chronology.detail: Later Chinese dynasty period; final Byzantine embassy recorded in 1081

chronology.label: Final Byzantine embassy to China
chronology.detail: Embassy by Michael VII Doukas arrived at Song court; recorded in History of Song

chronology.label: Yunnan bullion exports
chronology.detail: Gold and silver from Yunnan shipped via Burma (Ledo route) to Bangladesh

chronology.label: Mongol expansion
chronology.detail: Helped bring political stability; re-established Silk Road via Karakorum and Khanbaliq; ended Islamic Caliphate dominance

chronology.label: Yuan dynasty (Mongol China)
chronology.detail: Kublai Khan founded Yuan; Khanbaliq as capital; Mongol-sponsored business flourished

chronology.label: Rabban Bar Sauma in Europe
chronology.detail: Mongol diplomat visited European courts; provided detailed written reports

chronology.label: Treaty of Aleppo
chronology.detail: Ilkhanate Mongols converted to Islam; signed with Egyptian Mamluks

chronology.label: Ibn Battuta's travels
chronology.detail: Moroccan Muslim traveller crossed Silk Road from Tabriz

chronology.label: Death of Caterina Vilioni
chronology.detail: European (Venetian) sibling died in Yangzhou; tombstone found

chronology.label: Death of Antonio Vilioni
chronology.detail: European sibling died in Yangzhou; Europeans living in China for extended periods

chronology.label: Black Death begins in Europe
chronology.detail: May have originated from Central Asian marmots; carried westward by Silk Road traders via Trebizond

chronology.label: Ming dynasty
chronology.detail: Later Chinese dynasty; 1371 Hongwu Emperor sent proclamation to Byzantine court via merchant Nieh-ku-lun

chronology.label: Samarkand revival
chronology.detail: Turko-Mongol ruler Timur made Samarkand capital of Timurid Empire; moved artisans and intellectuals there

chronology.label: Ottoman control and Age of Discovery
chronology.detail: Ottoman Empire competed for control of overland routes; prompted European alternatives; began Age of Discovery

chronology.label: End of classical Silk Road era
chronology.detail: Marked by c. 1450 CE terminal date; shift to maritime routes and European colonialism

chronology.label: Safavid Empire collapse
chronology.detail: Persian silk trade disrupted; ended continuous silk trade legacy

chronology.label: Armenian monopoly on Persian silk exports
chronology.detail: Armenian merchants entirely conducted Persian silk exports; also raisins, coffee, figs, yarn, camel hair, stones, rice

chronology.label: Ferdinand von Richthofen popularizes 'Silk Road' term
chronology.detail: German term Seidenstraße coined; made seven China expeditions 1868-1872; term based on older usage

chronology.label: Sven Hedin publishes 'The Silk Road'
chronology.detail: Swedish geographer's book; first book with this title; term gains academic acceptance

chronology.label: UNESCO tourism development begins
chronology.detail: UN World Tourism Organization started sustainable international tourism development along Silk Road

chronology.label: UNESCO World Heritage Site designation
chronology.detail: Chang'an-Tianshan Corridor designated at 38th session; 2014 Conference on World Heritage

chronology.label: Silk Road Week commemoration
chronology.detail: China National Silk Museum announced Silk Road Week (June 19-25); Bishkek and Almaty named streets after Silk Road

chronology.label: Zarafshan-Karakum Corridor designated
chronology.detail: Second UNESCO World Heritage Site designation at 45th session

polities.name: Han dynasty
polities.relevance: Initiated Silk Road (202 BCE-220 CE); expanded into Central Asia; secured routes; established unified control

polities.name: Roman Empire
polities.relevance: Western terminus and major consumer market (30 BCE-3rd century CE); created demand for silk; developed ports and trade networks

polities.name: Later Han dynasty
polities.relevance: Continued Silk Road expansion; established security infrastructure; imperial envoys

polities.name: Parthian Empire
polities.relevance: Bridge connecting Silk Road to Mediterranean; vital intermediary; blocked some routes; traded with Romans and Chinese

polities.name: Xiongnu
polities.relevance: Nomadic tribes harassing Chinese; Han responded by opening protected routes; military competition and trade facilitation

polities.name: Greek Seleucids
polities.relevance: Earlier Hellenistic powers controlling parts of Central Asia routes

polities.name: Dayuan (Great Ionians)
polities.relevance: Greek kingdoms of Central Asia (Ferghana); bred heavenly horses; Han fought War of Heavenly Horses; early Silk Road partner

polities.name: Bactria / Bactrian Kingdom
polities.relevance: Greek-influenced Central Asian state; Greco-Bactrian rule remnants; major trade hub; merchants from

polities.name: Kushan Empire
polities.relevance: Unified Central Asia and Northern India (1st-3rd centuries); reinforced merchant role; enabled Buddhist transmission; cultural hoards

polities.name: Yuezhi
polities.relevance: Nomadic group; Zhang Qian sought alliance against Xiongnu; territories in Transoxiana

polities.name: Kangju
polities.relevance: Central Asian kingdom visited by Zhang Qian

polities.name: Silla Kingdom
polities.relevance: Korean state; received Roman artifacts via Silk Road (Gyeongju); benefited from maritime trade

polities.name: Sasanian Empire (Persia)
polities.relevance: Major power blocking direct trade; competed with Byzantines; controlled key routes; eventually declined

polities.name: Byzantine Empire
polities.relevance: Eastern Roman successor; continued western terminus role; sought silk production secrets; sent embassies; competed with Islamic powers

polities.name: First Turkic Khaganate
polities.relevance: Nomadic confederation; allied with Byzantines against Sasanians; formed Sogdian embassy (568)

polities.name: Tang dynasty
polities.relevance: Golden age of Silk Road (618-907 CE); reopened and secured routes; defeated Göktürks; established Pax Sinica; expanded maritime routes

polities.name: Tibetan Empire
polities.relevance: Periodically controlled Silk Road sections; alternated control with Tang; disrupted routes; contained Buddhism spread

polities.name: Sogdian merchants / Sogdiana
polities.relevance: Dominant middle-men traders (4th-8th centuries); lingua franca for Asian trade; facilitated all exchanges; pre-10th century merchants

polities.name: Göktürks
polities.relevance: Nomadic confederation; controlled steppes; competed with Tang; defeated by Li Jing

polities.name: Tuyuhun
polities.relevance: Nomadic confederation; targeted by Tang campaigns (640s-650s)

polities.name: Xueyantuo
polities.relevance: Nomadic confederation; targeted by Tang campaigns

polities.name: Umayyad Caliphate
polities.relevance: Islamic expansion into Central Asia (8th century); competed with Chinese; Battle of Talas (751) ended Chinese westward expansion

polities.name: Abbasid Caliphate
polities.relevance: Islamic empire; built Baghdad as major Silk Road hub; spread Islam along routes; competed with Chinese and Byzantines

polities.name: Persian Samanid Empire
polities.relevance: Centered in Bukhara (819-999); continued Sogdian trade legacy; maintained routes through Central Asia

polities.name: Kara-Khanid Khanate
polities.relevance: Turkic Islamic state; conquered Central Asia end of 10th century; replaced Buddhist and other religions with Islam

polities.name: Mongol Empire
polities.relevance: Vast political unification (c. 1207-1360); restored Silk Road security; facilitated unprecedented trade; unified zones previously separate

polities.name: Yuan dynasty
polities.relevance: Mongol rule of China (1271-1368); Khanbaliq as capital; Kublai Khan; maintained Mongol Silk Road hegemony

polities.name: Ilkhanate
polities.relevance: Mongol division in western Asia; controlled Middle East routes; converted to Islam; signed Treaty of Aleppo (1323)

polities.name: Song dynasty
polities.relevance: Chinese state (960-1279); existed during Mongol era; received Byzantine and other embassies; maritime trade center

polities.name: Ming dynasty
polities.relevance: Chinese state (1368-1644); claimed Silk Road legacy; sent envoys to Byzantine court; terrestrial decline toward maritime focus

polities.name: Timurid Empire
polities.relevance: Central Asian state (c. 1370+); Timur revived Samarkand as cultural and trade capital

polities.name: Safavid Empire
polities.relevance: Persian state; conducted extensive silk trade; Armenian merchants monopolized exports until collapse (1720s)

polities.name: Ottoman Empire
polities.relevance: Competed for control of overland routes from 1453 onwards; prompted European alternatives

polities.name: Maurya dynasty
polities.relevance: Indian empire; Emperor Ashoka converted to Buddhism; influenced religion's spread via Silk Road

polities.name: Radhanites / Radanite merchants
polities.relevance: Judean merchant network from Gaul; traded from China to Rome; facilitated east-west Jewish commerce

polities.name: Khazar Turks
polities.relevance: Nomadic confederation; served as middlemen between China and Rome for Radhanites; commercial partners

quotes.text: Thus more embassies were dispatched to Anxi [Parthia], Yancai [who later joined the Alans], Lijian [Syria under the Greek Seleucids], Tiaozhi (Mesopotamia), and Tianzhu [northwestern India] ... As a rule, rather more than ten such missions went forward in the course of a year, and at the least five or six.
quotes.speaker: Hou Hanshu (Later Han History)

quotes.text: [A] Han expedition into Central Asia, west of Jaxartes River, apparently encountered and defeated a contingent of Roman legionaries. The Romans may have been part of Antony's army invading Parthia. Sogdiana (modern Bukhara), east of the Oxus River, on the Polytimetus River, was apparently the most easterly penetration ever made by Roman forces in Asia. The margin of Chinese victory appears to have been their crossbows, whose bolts and darts seem easily to have penetrated Roman shields and armour.
quotes.speaker: Historical record (36 BCE)

quotes.text: I can see clothes of silk, if materials that do not hide the body, nor even one's decency, can be called clothes. ... Wretched flocks of maids labour so that the adulteress may be visible through her thin dress, so that her husband has no more acquaintance than any outsider or foreigner with his wife's body.
quotes.speaker: Seneca the Younger (Roman author)

quotes.text: The Son of Heaven on hearing all this reasoned thus: Ferghana (Dayuan "Great Ionians") and the possessions of Bactria (Ta-Hsia) and Parthian Empire (Anxi) are large countries, full of rare things, with a population living in fixed abodes and given to occupations somewhat identical with those of the Chinese people, but with weak armies, and placing great value on the rich produce of China
quotes.speaker: Hou Hanshu, Later Han History (attributed to Emperor Wu's reasoning)

quotes.text: They weave webs, like spiders, that become a luxurious clothing material for women, called silk.
quotes.speaker: Pliny the Elder (Natural Histories, on the bombyx/silk moth)

quotes.text: Regarding merchants who now sail from Egypt ... as far as the Ganges, they are only private citizens.
quotes.speaker: Strabo (1st-century Roman writer)

quotes.text: Many barbarian tribes became skilled warriors able to conquer rich cities and fertile lands and to forge strong military empires.
quotes.speaker: Historical account (paraphrased in p46)

quotes.text: According to historians, the main driving force of the Great Silk Road were not just Sogdians, but the carriers of a mixed Sogdian-Türkic culture that often came from mixed families.
quotes.speaker: A. V. Dybo (historian)
